Frozen-model history perturbations evaluated against training-prefix targets measure in-sample model reliance: how predictions change when fitted histories are shuffled, truncated or otherwise altered. They do not establish held-out next-item generalization; freezing weights does not undo prior exposure to targets. This interpretation follows the distinction between training-set and held-out permutation importance in the [scikit-learn documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/permutation_importance). Large perturbation effects can reflect memorization or unrealistic perturbed histories, so report them as sensitivity diagnostics rather than causal effects or expected validation gains.

For repeated prefixes, use paired user-cluster resampling: sample users with replacement within each category, retain all selected users’ prefixes and matched original/perturbed outcomes, and recompute the effect. Cluster resampling preserves within-user dependence; paired resampling preserves the comparison, as supported by [cluster-bootstrap research](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7148287/) and [SciPy’s paired-bootstrap definition](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.bootstrap.html). Specify whether users receive equal weight or longer histories contribute more. For the four-category macro statistic, recompute each category’s effect and average categories equally in every replicate.

These intervals describe diagnostic variability conditional on the fitted checkpoint and observed histories; they do not account for training randomness, search selection or eliminate in-sample bias. Repeated perturbations estimate additional perturbation randomness, not additional independent users. Keep generalization claims tied to the pinned held-out validation protocol and retain its fixed splits. Sequential-recommendation research shows that evaluation protocols and temporal leakage can materially change measured performance ([Ji et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11060)).
